title: The Series That Reached Pi
subtitle: When Numbers Chased Infinity on the Shores of Kerala
region: Kerala manuscripts of Tantrasangraha, Yuktibhasa and Yukti-dipika
moral: The infinite becomes powerful when it is made precise.

sources.citation: Jyeshthadeva, Yuktibhasa, c. 1530-1550, tr. K.V. Sarma et al. as Ganita-Yukti-Bhasa (2008)
sources.note: Malayalam proof-text giving derivations of the pi and trigonometric series.

sources.citation: Sankara Variyar, Yukti-dipika, verses on Madhava's sine series and Katapayadi pi value
sources.note: Preserves quoted Sanskrit verses attributed to Madhava.

sources.citation: Victor J. Katz, Mathematics Magazine 68:3 (1995); David Bressoud, College Mathematics Journal 33:1 (2002); Plofker (2009)
sources.note: Careful modern framing of Kerala series as precursors, not full calculus.

dialogue.text: On the sunlit coast of Kerala, Madhava’s school turned endless series into tools, binding pi and the stars to human hands.
Kerala in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries was a land of temple astronomy, busy ports, and learned houses where jyotisha and ganita served ritual, calendar, and sea.
In this world, Madhava of Sangamagrama had taught that the circle itself could be tamed by series, and his disciples now sought to record the reasons behind each rule.
In Tantrasangraha, Nīlakantha and others set out refined planetary models. But verses only hinted at deeper methods; Madhava’s innovations lay behind them like unseen machinery.
Jyeshthadeva answered with Yuktibhasa, a book of reasons, setting out in Malayalam the derivations of Madhava’s series for sine, cosine, arctangent, and pi.
He began from geometry, slicing the circle into finer arcs, showing how chords and tangents could be expressed by patterns of fractions repeating without end.
From Madhava came the insight that pi could be approached by an alternating arctangent series, where 1 minus 1 over 3 plus 1 over 5 and so on crept ever closer to pi over four.
He showed how to sum enough terms to get a good value, yet he knew the series moved slowly; without corrections, useful accuracy would demand too many steps.

panels.shot: medium shot with overlay of geometric sketch

dialogue.text: So the Kerala mathematicians devised clever error terms, estimating the tail beyond their last addition, turning infinity into a controlled tool rather than a vague idea.

dialogue.speaker: madhava_s_mathematical_school
dialogue.text: We must always ask: how far does this sum stray from the truth?

panels.shot: medium shot focusing on sine series

dialogue.text: For sine and cosine, he set out Madhava’s series in detail, linking geometric constructions to algebraic patterns, and giving explicit remainder bounds to decide when to stop.
Sankara Variyar’s Yukti-dipika preserved Sanskrit verses echoing these same ideas, crediting Madhava by name and tying the school together across generations of scribes.
In one Katapayadi verse, the tradition hid a value of pi accurate to eleven decimal places, a silent testament to the power of their series and corrections.
These were not idle games. Accurate sines and tangents fed tables that guided eclipse predictions, ritual timings, and even the reckoning of routes for coastal voyages.
Yet Jyeshthadeva did not claim to have a single grand theory of change. He worked case by case, careful proofs for particular functions, leaving later ages to weave broader fabric.

panels.shot: transition shot comparing manuscripts across cultures

dialogue.text: Centuries later, in distant Europe, similar infinite series would be rediscovered and linked into calculus. The Kerala work stood as an earlier strand, distinct yet astonishingly aligned.
The school’s legacy travelled not by conquest but by copying: palm leaves dried, etched, and passed on, each preserving elaborate chains of reasoning in a regional tongue.
From Madhava to Jyeshthadeva, the Kerala school showed that infinity could be approached, bounded, and harnessed, proving that the infinite becomes powerful only when made precise.
